title: Death and dying, closed
hookLine: certain, uncertain, and the practice that helps
tomorrow: what happens when you get what you want, and when you don't?

cards: Ask a table of friends what happens after we die, and the debate starts before the food arrives. Somebody is sure. Somebody laughs it off.
Somebody goes quiet. An old story puts that whole table into four short answers, given by a weaver's daughter to the Buddha in front of a crowd. And the crowd thinks she's being rude.

teach.b: The story comes from the Dhammapada commentary. In the town of Alavi, the Buddha had taught a simple reflection: my life is uncertain, my death is certain. Later he asks the girl four questions.
Where have you come from? I don't know. Where are you going?
I don't know. Don't you know? I know.
Do you know? I don't know. People mutter.
Then she explains. I don't know where I was before this birth. I don't know where I'll go after it.

teach.h: I KNOW I WILL DIE. NOT WHEN.
teach.b: I know I will die. I don't know when. The Buddha praises every answer.
The commentary adds a hard ending: later that day, at her father's loom, she dies in an accident. Certain, and uncertain. Now the debate, because Buddhists read the unknown part in more than one way.
Some say rebirth and kamma are plainly part of the teaching.
Their best case: she didn't doubt that she was going somewhere, only where, and that long view is what makes each act matter.
Others lean on a sutta where the Buddha speaks to the Kalamas, townspeople unsure whom to trust. Their best case: he offers assurances for both possibilities.
If there is a next life and deeds bear fruit, a kind life goes well. If there isn't, a person free of hatred lives at ease here and now. Practice doesn't wait for certainty.
Notice where the two sides meet. Neither says the time is known. Both send you back to the same place: this life, now.

how: The weaver's daughter's story is told in Theravada teaching on reflection on death, with the line 'life is uncertain, death is certain'; Buddhists of different schools hold rebirth with different emphasis, and teachers sometimes cite the Kalama Sutta's assurances for those still unsure.

o: the moment the mind leaves the body for good
a festival honoring ancestors once each year
the certain fact of death, and its unknown time

games.q: her four answers — tap the pairs.
p: I don't know: before this birth
I don't know: after this life

s: the crowd at Alavi thought the girl was being disrespectful
her short answers sounded rude until she explained them, and the Buddha praised each one.
every Buddhist holds rebirth in exactly the same way
some hold it as plainly taught; others practice with the Kalama assurances, good either way.

games.q: a friend says rebirth is the whole point of the path. you lean toward the Kalama assurances. what's her best case, in her own terms?
o: she knows she's going somewhere, so every act has a long reach.
rebirth is comforting, so it helps people stop worrying.
the Buddha never mentioned rebirth, so she's adding it in.
games.why: the weaver's daughter doubted only where she'd go, not whether. for those who hold rebirth plainly, that long view is what gives each act weight. the Kalama side has its own best case: practice doesn't wait for certainty.

practice: Rest one hand open on your knee. With each slow breath, fold in one finger for one plain gift this life gave you today: a meal, a voice, warm water, light through a window.
When the hand is closed, open it again and keep counting until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Death and dying: a whole block on the one thing that's certain and the many that aren't. The block closes on a girl's honest answers.

orig.note: Pali: death. In the reflection: life uncertain, maraṇa certain.

carryVoice: Keep this one: this life, now, and the rest can stay an open question. Death and dying, closed.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary (Dhammapada-atthakatha) on verse 174: the weaver's daughter of Alavi
